after.worked_solution:
Here, both the lower and upper limits contain a variable. However, to apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit only. So, we can split the integral into two integrals, and rewrite them so that in both cases the variable is on the upper limit. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{x}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}\sqrt[3]{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{x}^{a}\sqrt[3]{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}\sqrt[3]{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{a}^{x}\sqrt[3]{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}\sqrt[3]{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a$ is any constant number between $x$ and $\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$

The integrand $\sqrt[3]{1+{t}^{2}}$ is continuous for all $t,$ so applying FTC II gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{a}^{x}\sqrt[3]{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}\sqrt[3]{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{x}\sqrt[3]{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\sqrt[3]{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\sqrt[3]{1+{x}^{2}}+\frac{\text{du}}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({\int }_{a}^{u}\sqrt[3]{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\sqrt[3]{1+{x}^{2}}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))\sqrt[3]{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\sqrt[3]{1+(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))^{2}}-\sqrt[3]{1+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\sqrt[3]{1+{sin}^{2}⁡(x)}-\sqrt[3]{1+{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$

Finally, we can compute ${F}^{′}(0).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(0) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\sqrt[3]{1+{sin}^{2}⁡(0)}-\sqrt[3]{1+(0)^{2}} \\  & =1\sqrt[3]{1}-\sqrt[3]{1} \\  & =1-1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, both the lower and upper limits contain a variable. However, to apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit only. So, we can split the integral into two integrals, and rewrite them so that in both cases the variable is on the upper limit. We get ∫xsin⁡(x)1+t23dt=∫xa1+t23dt+∫asin⁡(x)1+t23dt=−∫ax1+t23dt+∫asin⁡(x)1+t23dt, where a is any constant number between x and sin⁡x.

Note that we used the substitution u=sin⁡x.

F′(0)=cos⁡(0)1+sin2⁡(0)3−1+(0)23=113−13=1−1=0.

after.problem: Let $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)-x.$ Find ${g}^{′}(2)$ given the function is defined by $g(x)={\int }_{x}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t.$
after.worked_solution:
In this example, the variable limit $x$ is located on the lower limit. To apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit. Using the properties of definite integrals, we can write

$$
g(x)={\int }_{x}^{0}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)-t)\,\text{d}t=-{\int }_{0}^{x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)-t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, by FTC II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{x}^{0}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)-t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{0}^{x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)-t)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{0}^{x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)-t)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)-x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the value of ${g}^{′}(2),$ we substitute $x=2$ in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(2) & =-(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot 2)-2) \\  & =-(0-2) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
To compute ${f}^{′}(x),$ we first make the substitution $u={x}^{2}$ and then we apply the chain rule, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}t\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{0}^{u}t\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

The integrand is continuous on $[0,u],$ and so by FTC II we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot u\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{u} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})\cdot u\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{u} \\  & =2x\cdot {x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{{x}^{2}} \\  & =2{x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute ${f}^{′}(x),$ we first make the substitution $u=3x-5$ and then we apply the chain rule, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{3x-5}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{u}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

The limit $u$ is located on the lower limit. To apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit. Using the properties of the definite integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{u}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(-{\int }_{1}^{u}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{1}^{u}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by FTC II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot (-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{1}^{u}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2u-1)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3x-5)\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2u-1)) \\  & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(3x-5)-1) \\  & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x-11).\end{aligned}
$$

Find f′(0) if f(x)=∫x3x+2(6t−7)dt.

a
7ln⁡3
b
11ln⁡3+7
c
4ln⁡3−5
d
2ln⁡3−1
e
6ln⁡3+5

decision.explanation: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, f′(x)=[6(3^x+2)-7]3^x ln(3)-(6x-7). At x=0, this gives f′(0)=11 ln(3)+7.

after.worked_solution:
Here, both the lower and upper limits contain a variable. However, to apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit only. So, we can split the integral into two integrals, and rewrite them so that in both cases the variable is on the upper limit. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{x}^{{3}^{x}+2}(6t-7)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{x}^{a}(6t-7)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{{3}^{x}+2}(6t-7)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{a}^{x}(6t-7)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{{3}^{x}+2}(6t-7)\,\text{d}t,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a$ is any constant number between $x$ and ${3}^{x}+2.$

The integrand $(6t-7)$ is continuous for all $t,$ so applying the FTC II gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{a}^{x}(6t-7)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{{3}^{x}+2}(6t-7)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{x}(6t-7)\,\text{d}t)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{{3}^{x}+2}(6t-7)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-(6x-7)+\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({\int }_{a}^{u}(6t-7)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =7-6x+({3}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3))(6u-7) \\  & =7-6x+({3}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3))(6({3}^{x}+2)-7) \\  & =7-6x+({3}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3))(6\cdot {3}^{x}+5).\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the substitution $u={3}^{x}+2.$

Finally, we can compute ${f}^{′}(0).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(0) & =7-6(0)+({3}^{0}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3))(6\cdot {3}^{0}+5) \\  & =7+11\operatorname{ln}⁡(3).\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Here, both the lower and upper limits contain a variable. However, to apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit only. So, we can split the integral into two integrals, and rewrite them so that in both cases the variable is on the upper limit. We get ∫x3x+2(6t−7)dt=∫xa(6t−7)dt+∫a3x+2(6t−7)dt=−∫ax(6t−7)dt+∫a3x+2(6t−7)dt, where a is any constant number between x and 3x+2.

The integrand (6t−7) is continuous for all t, so applying the FTC II gives f′(x)=ddx(−∫ax(6t−7)dt+∫a3x+2(6t−7)dt)=−ddx(∫ax(6t−7)dt)+ddx(∫a3x+2(6t−7)dt)=−(6x−7)+dudxddu(∫au(6t−7)dt)=7−6x+(3xln⁡(3))(6u−7)=7−6x+(3xln⁡(3))(6(3x+2)−7)=7−6x+(3xln⁡(3))(6⋅3x+5).

Note that we used the substitution u=3x+2.

Finally, we can compute f′(0). We get f′(0)=7−6(0)+(30ln⁡(3))(6⋅30+5)=7+11ln⁡(3).
